title: A Student’s Presentation on What Children Can See on School-Issued Devices
author: Emily Cherkin
summary: Emily Cherkin shares slides that a Maine middle schooler built for their school board and assistant superintendent, documenting what students can reach on school-issued laptops. The student shows an AI image tool producing graphic images from a mild prompt "with no end," AI tools used in class and testing, a tool that "humanizes" AI-written text to dodge detection, and three ways students bypass Wi-Fi filters (hotspots, a teacher's Wi-Fi, home Wi-Fi). Cherkin adds that games slip past blocks by posing as educational sites. She protects the child by removing identifying details and notes the district responded with a tepid promise to "collect more screentime data." She ties the episode to a new lawsuit over Google Gemini on a school Chromebook and closes by asking why leaders will not simply listen to students.
points: Student-collected evidence shows school filters and "blocked" lists fail in practice, because students route around them through hotspots, teacher Wi-Fi, home Wi-Fi and VPNs.
Generative AI apps on school devices can produce graphic content from innocuous prompts, which makes access control a safeguarding issue rather than a settings issue.
Students also use school-provided AI tools to write and then "humanize" assignments, so detection filters are always a step behind.
The district answered with a call for more screentime data instead of a change in access, which Cherkin reads as adults declining to act on evidence in front of them.
Cherkin's remedy is cheap and immediate: ask students what they can access and take their testimony seriously.
quotes: If any of the following slides make you uncomfortable, I ask you to imagine all of this district’s kids having access to them. That includes your kids.

Though the reaction of the adults should have been one of outrage, shock, and awe at what children are able to access on their school laptops, the student instead received a tepid response and a weak promise to “collect more screentime data” before the district would make any decisions on access changes.

I have left the slides exactly the way the student put them in the presentation because if a child is able to access this on their school-issued device then adults should be forced to look at them and sit with that.
The kids are alway, always, always one (or more) steps ahead of us. Here is how this student made an AI-written paragraph sound more “human”— using an AI tool available on their school device.

Children are always more technologically-savvy than the adults around them. It is foolish for school leaders to think that blocks and filters will actually prevent students from accessing sites and content they want to access.
Schools cannot hand children internet-connected devices and expect children not to get tempted to look for and play games that will tap into their neural pathways.
I would be very curious to know if any school leadership or board directors know how to do any of this, or even that this is possible on student devices.
I’m not sure what more school leaders need in order to act. Maybe try listening to their students?
